s07.slug: FRIDAY · 11:20 PM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: Since Thursday the strand around her window has lost more ground. What still burns has pulled back into the bottom right corner of the frame, a knot of red and green and one white gone stubborn yellow, so the light in her room comes up off the sill from one side, low, like footlights somebody quit hanging halfway through.

They came in by the alley. The rack is where it was, and the jar of beach glass with the blue piece on top, and the O’Connor on the sill with CON struck through. The floor has been picked up since Thursday; his shirt isn’t on it. The white dress still hangs on the back of the door in the cleaner’s bag, its collar standing up under the paper. Skye lifts it off the hook by the hanger and hangs it on the rack between two flannels, and pats the bag once.
“She’s had a big week,” she says.
“Second time anybody’s been up here,” she says over her shoulder. “You’re a regular. It’s alarming.”
She takes his right hand and turns it over under the lights. The Lava got the backs of it. The black is still packed under every nail, ten thin crescents of her battery.
“You washed.”
“There was soap.”
“Most of my car’s still on you,” Skye says, and keeps the hand.

She wants the party, all of it, from the door. He gives it to her sitting on the end of the mattress with his boots off and her feet in his lap: the priest at the door in a cardigan, who took one look and knew he’d pushed a car; the organist at the upright with a voice like a foghorn, a measure behind on every verse and not sorry; a parish secretary, seventy-one, three cups into a punch somebody from Texas had done something to, sailing the descant a third above everybody; the priest tasting the punch and putting the bowl on top of the refrigerator. His roommate’s spray tan, unopened, going home with the priest. He leaves out the upright, and the kitchen doorway, and what was hanging in it. She watches his face go past that part, and lets it go by.
“Do her,” Skye says. “The secretary.”
“You’ve never heard her.”

“Do I need to?” She stands up on the mattress in her socks with one hand on the window frame and her chin in the air, and sings *Joy to the world* a third above anywhere it has ever lived, with a quaver in it like a kettle coming up and the total confidence of three cups, and holds the last note until the frame creaks under her hand. It’s terrible. It’s not far off.

He tells her the white elephant: a girl with a clipboard running it like an auction, steals allowed, three steals and it’s frozen. A kid named Joey got her bag, bow and all, and shook the 8-Ball with his eyes shut and asked it if he was going to be a priest, and it said *It is decidedly so*, and the room went up like somebody had scored. And then there were steals.

body.text: “Did they read the tag?” “To the room. *From St. Nicholas.*” “Did he get a laugh?” “He got a look.” “Range,” Skye says.

body: “It *is* decided,” Skye says, and sits down hard beside him with her knees up. “I told you. Every answer.” She bumps him with her shoulder. “So who got my Eight Ball?”

response: “A friend,” he says.
“In italics?”
He says nothing. She looks at him over her knees with her head on one side, long enough that he knows she heard it, and lets it be.

choices.text: “Joey. The one who’s going to be a priest.”
response: “Joey,” he says. “The one who’s going to be a priest.”
“Then it told the truth once,” Skye says. “That’s a good career for a toy.”
“It went to a good home.”
“What did they ask it?”
“They didn’t say.”
“Smart,” Skye says. “Never tell anybody your question. They give you notes on it.”

s07a.slug: FRIDAY · 11:45 PM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: By a quarter to twelve his flannel and her sweater are on the floor with the scripts, and she’s lying on top of him in a black bra and her jeans with her chin on her stacked hands in the middle of his chest, looking at him down her nose, what’s left of the lights in the side of her hair.
“I’ve been doing coverage on your sentence,” she says.
“Coverage.”

“It’s what readers do. You read the script and write two pages on why it doesn’t work.” She takes one hand out from under her chin and holds up a finger. “One. It isn’t a rule. You said so yourself — not always, not till marriage, you don’t know that about you. A rule I’d respect. I’ve worked union.” A second finger. “So it’s a schedule. And a person’s allowed to ask what’s on a schedule. That’s what a schedule is *for*.”
“It’s not a schedule. It’s a no.”
“It’s a no with a date on it.”
“I didn’t put a date on it.”

“You put *now* on it. Now is the most specific date there is.” She taps his breastbone on *now*. “You people have a candle for rejoicing and a Sunday it’s due. You told me so. Don’t lie there and tell me Catholics don’t keep a calendar.”

She rolls off him long enough to unbutton her jeans and work them down her legs and kick them off the end of the mattress, and rolls back on, and doesn’t lose her place. “Costume change. Two. It had a time on it. A quarter past four, Friday morning. That was nineteen and a half hours ago. I’ve done live television, Jack. *Now* lasts about four seconds. After that it’s a rerun.”

A third finger. “And in my business you never shoot the white pages. Every rewrite comes out on a new color — blue, pink, yellow, green. By the time anybody rolls camera it’s goldenrod. Right now was a white page.” She folds her hands back under her chin. “We’re on blue. Possibly pink.”
He laughs, and it moves her up and down on his chest, and she rides it out and waits.

“Four.” She reaches behind her own back with both hands, without hurrying and without taking her eyes off his, and the bra goes over the edge of the mattress after the jeans, and she settles her chin back on her hands as if nothing in the room has changed. “Visual aids.”
Nothing in the room is the same. She knows it. She lets him find that out, all of it, the lights on her skin and her heart going against his chest, before she goes on.

“Exhibit A. Thursday, on this mattress, you said, and I’m quoting, *I’ve wanted you since the window seat.*” She lays one finger flat on his chest. “And at a quarter past four you told me it isn’t me you don’t trust. It’s you. So I took a meeting with you. Two weeks of notes. You pushed my car in Buellton. You stood in my rain. You’ve been in my bed twice and you’re still wearing a belt.” She tips her head. “Jack. You are the most trustworthy man who has ever been underneath me.”
“That’s not evidence.”
“It’s *coverage*.”

It’s a good argument. Most of it is better than good. He can’t find the hole in it from underneath her, and that may be why she made it from up there, and she’s funny, which is worse, because he’s laughing and he wants her and the two have got into each other and won’t come apart.

“So the notes are in,” Skye says. “The sentence doesn’t work. We’re on new pages.” She smiles down at him, slow, and her hand goes down between them to his belt, sure of itself, the way it went Thursday — and this time she says it out loud, because she has made her case and she knows it was a good one. “Is it still right now?”

choices.key: Friday night she took your “right now” apart and asked if it was still right now. You put your hand over hers on the buckle again and said no.
response: His hand goes down and covers hers on the buckle, the way it did Thursday, and stops it there.
“It’s still right now,” he says. “No.”

choices.key: Friday night she took your “right now” apart, and nearly won. You told her you want her, and it’s still no.
response: “I want you,” he says. “Every page of it. It’s still no.”

choices.key: Friday night she took your “right now” apart, and nearly won. You told her: still the white pages, still no.
response: “Still the white pages,” he says. “I don’t care what color you’re on. Still no.”

s07b.slug: FRIDAY · 11:50 PM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: She doesn’t argue the point she just lost. Her hand comes off his belt and goes back where it was before she started making her case — flat on his chest, over his heart — and stays there.
“A no’s a no. For tonight. For that.” She smiles when she says it, pleased, a professional with a note she can play — and she doesn’t stop.

She goes back to her mark. Wherever they were before she opened her mouth, she goes back to it exactly, the way an actor walks back to the tape for another take, and picks it up from there. The jeans stay on the floor with the scripts, and the bra on the far side of the mattress, where the argument left them. She doesn’t take one step past where they were when the argument started. She doesn’t need to.

She’s easy in it — easy the way she is barefoot on a gas-station floor, or walking into the Pacific in November — in nothing now but a pair of black cotton underwear and the braided anklet, and he’s still in his jeans with the belt done up. She has always been at home in her skin, and tonight there’s a great deal of it.

Her mouth on his, slow, and then not slow. Her hair coming out of its knot and down over both their faces, so the room is a tent of it with the last of the lights coming through. The window is cold on one of her shoulders and the rest of her is heat. Her breasts on his chest, and her heart going under them, fast, right on top of his. He finds the freckles that go on down over her shoulders, more than her face has, and puts his mouth on them, and she tips her head back for it and makes a sound he hasn’t heard out of her before, low, nothing like a laugh.

When she comes up on her hands to look at him there are smudges down her ribs where his fingers have been — gray, from under his nails, her own battery — and she looks down at herself in the red light and laughs. “You’re getting my car on me.” She rubs one with her thumb and makes it worse, and comes back down.
Her hands stay where they were at a quarter to twelve: his hair, his shoulders, his ribs. Not one inch lower than that, all night.
“I’m not doing anything,” she says against his throat, doing it — doing exactly what she was doing before she ever said the word *coverage*.

She pulls the blanket up over both their heads, and under it there’s no light at all, only her, the heat of her and her breath and the salt at her hairline, and the braided anklet scratching at his shin through the denim. Her teeth find his shoulder. The muscles of her back move under his hands, and at the dip of her spine her skin has gone damp, and when he spreads his fingers there she presses back into them hard. He wants her so much it’s a sound in his ears, under the surf, and with her lying on him there’s no hiding it, and she wouldn’t let him if he tried.

Once she stops, and lies with her forehead on his, both of them breathing like they’ve run the stairs up the bluff, and he thinks that’s the end of it. She starts again from the top, slower, with all night to do it in. Her hands are in his hair; she pulls his head back by it, not gently, to look at him in what light there is, and whatever she finds in his face makes her smile, and he feels the smile against his mouth before he sees it.

There’s no question in any of it. That’s what he can’t get past, under her. She asked, and she argued it well, and he said no, and she put the thing he turned down back exactly where she found it and hasn’t gone near it since. There’s nothing left to say no to. There’s only everything they were already doing, and the whole night to do it in, and she is in no hurry at all.

His breathing has gone loud in the room, louder than the surf at the foot of the bluff and the stereo three houses down. She lifts her head and laughs at him, low and delighted. “Breathe, Jack,” she says. “That one’s allowed.”

body.text: He isn’t trying to be good. For a stretch of it he isn’t trying anything. There’s her mouth, and the heat coming off her, and her hands in his hair, and his own hands going places he’ll have to say on Saturday through a screen. His thoughts come shorter. Her skin. Her breath. Her skin. She never once moves toward the line. It’s his own body that keeps leaning at it, and the line holds anyway. It holds because he holds it, and it hurts.
body.else: Under all of it a voice he knows for his own keeps track, low and level. It doesn’t need to raise itself. She isn’t going anywhere near the line. The voice is keeping an eye on him.

choices.key: To the letter: she stopped where you said no, and nowhere else. You got up for water and stood at her window till it cooled.
response: “Water,” he says, and gets up.

There’s a bathroom at the end of the hall with a toothbrush glass on the sink. He fills it and brings it back and doesn’t drink it. He stands at her window with it and his back to her, bare to the waist, with the cold coming in under the sash and the surf down at the bottom of the bluff, and gives the cold a minute of him. She lets him have the minute.
When he turns around she’s under the blanket with it up to her chin, watching him.
“Better?”
“No.”
“Good,” Skye says, and lifts the edge of the blanket, and when he gets back in beside her in his jeans it has cooled enough to talk.

Somewhere inside the wall something goes *pop*, small and definite. The last knot of Christmas lights dies, and the line of light under the door dies with it, and three houses down the music keeps on while this house goes black from the roof to the alley. For the length of one wave there’s nothing in it but the surf.
Then her laugh in the dark, close to his ear.
“Unbelievable,” Skye says. “You converted the house.”
She finds a flashlight by feel, in one of the boots under the rack, and clicks it on and points it at the ceiling, and they lie there in the circle of it.

choices.key: To the letter: she stopped where you said no, and nowhere else. You told her it was cruel. She said thorough.
response: “This is cruel,” he says into her hair. It comes out hoarse.
“Cruel’s a strong word,” Skye says. “I’m being *thorough*.”

And then she’s laughing at her own line, at him, at the state of him, and she can’t stop, and she has to roll off him onto her back to do it properly with both hands over her face, and the laugh does what his no didn’t: by the time she’s finished with it the room has come down to something he can lie next to.

She finds a flashlight by feel, in one of the boots under the rack, and clicks it on and points it at the ceiling, and they lie there in the circle of it.

choices.key: To the letter: she stopped where you said no, and went no further. You let everything else run, and the line held.
response: He lets her. He stops keeping her anywhere — stops counting, takes his hand off the brake — and lets everything she’s allowed have all of him, and for a long time there’s nothing else. She never once goes near the thing he turned down. She doesn’t have to. By the end it takes everything he’s got to keep the line where he put it, and it’s his own hands he has to keep there, not hers, and none of it is easy, and he keeps it.

s07c.slug: SATURDAY · 1:00 AM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM, IN THE DARK
body: By one o’clock there’s a candle going in a jelly jar on the floor and the flashlight has given up beside it. The fuse box is in the darkroom. “I’m not allowed in the darkroom,” Skye says. “House rule. Something about the light getting in.” She’s in her flannel and he’s back in his undershirt, and they sit against the wall under the dead window with the blanket over their knees, and the candle makes the room about the size of the candle.

She asks what he’s doing in four hours, and he tells her: the old Mission on Mission Street, at five. A guy from work asked him to come hear his mother sing. It’s the feast — today, now; midnight went by while the lights were still on. Our Lady of Guadalupe. At five in the morning they sing her *Las Mañanitas*, the birthday song, with a mariachi, and bank roses around her picture till you can smell them from the street.
“Why roses?”

So he tells her the part everybody knows. A hill outside Mexico City, in December, a long time ago. A man on his way to Mass, and a lady on the hill who sent him to the bishop. The bishop wanted a sign. She sent the man back up the hill for roses, in December, where nothing grows, and he carried them down in his coat, and when he opened the coat in front of the bishop the roses fell out on the floor and she was on the cloth.
Skye sits up off the wall. “Wait. Green cape? Stars all over it? Gold coming off her in spikes?”
“That’s her.”

“She’s on every taco truck in the Valley. She’s on the tall candles at the liquor store on Ventura. There’s a wall of her on Lankershim by a car wash, twenty feet high.” She looks at him across the candle. “I thought she was a *brand*.”
“She’s Our Lady.”
“The worth-something-first lady?” “Same lady.”
“Who painted her?”
“No one. That’s the story.”

She sits with that longer than he expects, chin on her knees. “The bishop’s the only one in it I believe,” she says at last. “Somebody pitches him a miracle and he asks to see it on tape.” She turns her head on her knees to look at him. “Whoever lit her knew what they were doing.”
“That’s the idea,” Jack says.
“I’ll drive you,” she says. “Mission’s on my way to the freeway. I want to see the candles from the car.” And then, in the same breath: “When do you tell your priest about me?”
“This afternoon. Three-thirty.”

“Do you get points for tonight?” She puts up a hand to stop him answering, drops her voice down into her chest and flattens every vowel in it, and she’s a patient man from Ohio explaining something in a parked car: “It doesn’t work like points.”
“It doesn’t.”
“I heard you the first time.” She reaches over and turns the jar so the flame stands up straight. “Tell him I was respectful.”
A little before three he asks her to set her alarm for half past four.
“Why?”
“So I’d leave.”

She tips her head at him over her knees. Then she fishes the white iPhone out of the boot where it lives and sets the alarm, and lays it on the floor by the candle, and goes back to the story she was in the middle of — a hamburger commercial she shot at twelve in a field in Simi Valley, in a hoopskirt, which she still won’t explain.

Somewhere after half past three he falls asleep sitting up against the wall. The marimba goes at four-thirty, bright and idiotic in the dark, and when he opens his eyes she’s where she was, knees up, the candle down in its own wax, looking at him.
“You fold your hands,” she says. “When you sleep. I watched you the entire hour. You look like a knight on a tomb.”

s08.slug: SATURDAY · 4:50 AM · THE SAAB, MISSION STREET
body: She puts the top up for the cold. The canvas comes over them stiff with damp and latches at the windshield, the heater runs full blast, her bare feet on the pedals, cold or not, and Mission Street at ten to five is wet black asphalt with the signals going through their colors down the grade toward the harbor and not a car to stop.
At the light by the Greyhound depot he switches the RAZR on. It finds a bar and buzzes once in his hand.
It sits on the outer screen, four hours old. He shuts the phone on it and puts it in the Carhartt. Skye downshifts for the light.

She pulls in at the curb two blocks short, by the depot bench under its caged tube of light. From there the Mission is up the street on the far side with every one of its doors open, and the doors are full of light — candles, a great many of them, and behind the candles a red that has to be roses, banked so deep the color carries two blocks. People are going in out of the dark in coats. Somewhere inside a trumpet tries a note and thinks better of it.
“That’s her?”
“That’s her.”
Skye looks with both hands on the wheel and the heater going, her face lit faintly from up the street.
“Is it rude? Watching from the car?”
“People watch her from the back all the time. She doesn’t mind.”
Skye takes that in, and nods at the doors, once, as if to somebody across a room she’s been introduced to.
“It’s yours,” she says. “I’ll watch the light come up from the freeway.”
She kisses him once, across the gearshift, her hand on the back of his neck, warm from the heater.
“Cassidy has a Saturday,” she says against his mouth. “There’s a Santa involved. Don’t ask.”

He gets out into the cold. She swings the Saab around in the empty street in one wide U across both lanes and goes back the way they came, toward the freeway and Los Angeles, and he walks the two blocks up toward the open doors with his hands in the Carhartt and the trumpet starting over inside, for real this time.
